{{Short description|Square roots of the eigenvalues of the self-adjoint operator A* A}}
In [[mathematics]], in particular in [[functional analysis]], the '''singular values''' of a [[compact operator]] <math>\, T \! : X \rightarrow Y</math> acting between [[Hilbert space]]s <math>X</math> and {{tmath|Y}}, are the square roots of the (necessarily non-negative) [[eigenvalue]]s of the [[self-adjoint operator]] <math>T^* T</math> (where <math>T^*</math> denotes the [[Adjoint operator|adjoint]] of {{tmath|T}}).

The singular values are non-negative [[real number]]s, usually listed in decreasing order {{tmath|\big( \sigma_{1}(T) \geq \sigma_{2}(T) \geq \dots \big)}}. The largest singular value <math>\sigma_{1}(T)</math> is equal to the [[operator norm]] of <math>T</math> (see [[Min-max theorem#Min-max principle for singular values|Min-max theorem]]).

[[File:Singular value decomposition.gif|thumb|right|280px|Visualization of a [[singular value decomposition]] (SVD) of a {{math|2}}-dimensional, real [[:en:Shear mapping|shearing matrix]] {{mvar|M}}. First, we see the [[unit disc]] in blue together with the two [[Standard basis|canonical unit vectors]]. We then see the action of {{mvar|M}}, which distorts the disc to an [[ellipse]]. The SVD decomposes {{mvar|M}} into three simple transformations: a [[Rotation matrix|rotation]] {{math|''V''{{sup|*}}}}, a [[Scaling (geometry)|scaling]] {{mvar|Σ}} along the rotated coordinate axes, and a second rotation {{mvar|U}}. Moreover, {{mvar|Σ}} is a (square, in this example) [[diagonal matrix]] containing in its diagonal the singular values of {{mvar|M}}, which represent the lengths {{math|''σ''<sub>1</sub>}} and {{math|''σ''<sub>2</sub>}} of the [[Ellipse#Elements of an ellipse|semi-axes]] of the ellipse.]]

If <math>T</math> acts on a [[Euclidean space]] (for example, {{tmath|\R^n}}), there is a simple geometric interpretation for the singular values: Consider the image by <math>T</math> of the [[N-sphere|unit sphere]]; this is an [[ellipsoid]], and the lengths of its semi-axes are the singular values of <math>T</math> (the figure provides an example in {{tmath|\R^2}}).

If {{tmath|A}} is a [[normal matrix]], then its singular values are the absolute values of its [[eigenvalues]]. Indeed, in this case, the [[spectral theorem]] can be applied to obtain unitary diagonalization of <math>A</math> as {{tmath|A {{=}} U \varLambda \, U^*}}. Then, by definition, {{tmath|\textstyle \sqrt{A^* A} {{=}} U \sqrt{\varLambda^* \varLambda} ~ U^* {{=}} U \, \vert \varLambda \vert ~ U^*}}.

Most [[Normed linear space|norms]] on Hilbert space operators studied are defined using singular values. For example, the [[Ky Fan]] {{tmath|k}}-norm is the sum of the first <math>k</math> singular values, the trace norm is the sum of all singular values, and the [[Schatten norm]] is the {{tmath|p}}-th root of the sum of the {{tmath|p}}-th powers of the singular values. Note that each norm is defined only on a special class of operators, hence singular values can be useful in classifying different operators.

In the finite-dimensional case, a [[Matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] can always be decomposed in the form {{tmath|U \varSigma \, V^*}}, where <math>U</math> and <math>V^*</math> are [[unitary matrices]] and <math>\varSigma</math> is a [[rectangular diagonal matrix]] with the singular values lying on its diagonal. This is the [[singular value decomposition]].

== Basic properties ==
For <math>A \in \C^{m \times n}</math> and {{tmath|i {{=}} 1,2, \ldots, \min \{ m,n \} }}:

[[Min-max theorem#Min-max principle for singular values|Min-max theorem for singular values]]:<br>Here, <math>U</math> is a subspace of {{tmath|\C^n}};

:<math>\sigma_i (A) = \min_{\dim(U)=n-i+1} \max_{\underset{\| x \|_2 = 1}{x \in U}} \left\| Ax \right\|_2.</math>
:<math>\sigma_i (A) = \max_{\dim(U)=i} \min_{\underset{\| x \|_2 = 1}{x \in U}} \left\| Ax \right\|_2.</math>

Matrix transpose and conjugate do not alter singular values:

:{{tmath|\sigma_i (A) {{=}} \sigma_i \! \left( A^\textsf{T} \right) {{=}} \sigma_i \! \left( A^* \right)}}.

For any unitary matrices <math>U \in \C^{m \times m}</math> and {{tmath|V \in \C^{n \times n} }},

:{{tmath|\sigma_i (A) {{=}} \sigma_i (UAV)}}.

Relation to eigenvalues:

:{{tmath|\sigma_i ^2 (A) {{=}} \lambda_i \! \left( A A^* \right) {{=}} \lambda_i \! \left( A^* A \right)}}.

Relation to [[Trace (linear algebra)|trace]]:

:{{tmath|\sum_{i{{=}}1}^n \sigma_i ^2 {{=}} \text{tr} (A^* A)}}.

If <math>A^* A</math> has full rank, the product of singular values is {{tmath|\det \sqrt{A^* A} }}.

If <math>A A^*</math> has full rank, the product of singular values is {{tmath|\det \sqrt{A A^*} }}.

If <math>A</math> is square and has full rank, the product of singular values is {{tmath|\vert \! \det A \vert}}.

If <math>A</math> is [[Normal matrix|normal]], then {{tmath|\sigma_i (A) {{=}} \left\vert \lambda_i (A) \right\vert}}, that is, its singular values are the absolute values of its eigenvalues.

For a generic rectangular {{tmath|m \times n}} matrix {{tmath|A}}, let <math display="inline">\tilde{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & A \\ A^* & 0 \end{bmatrix}</math> be its [[Augmented matrix|augmented]] {{tmath|(m+n) \times (m+n)}} matrix. {{tmath|2 \min \{ m,n \} }} eigenvalues of {{tmath|\tilde A}} are <math display="inline">\pm \sigma_i (A)</math> (where the <math display="inline">\sigma_i (A)</math> are the singular values of {{tmath|A}}), and the <math>|m-n|</math> remaining eigenvalues of {{tmath|\tilde A}} are zero. Let <math>A = U \varSigma \, V^*</math> be the singular value decomposition of {{tmath|A}}; then the eigenvectors of <math display="inline">\tilde{A}</math> for {{tmath|\pm \sigma_i (A)}} are {{tmath|\begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{u}_i \\ \pm \mathbf{v}_i \end{bmatrix} }}.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Tao |first=Terence |title=Topics in random matrix theory |date=2012 |publisher=American Mathematical Society |isbn=978-0-8218-7430-1 |series=Graduate studies in mathematics |location=Providence, R.I.}}</ref>{{Pg|page=52}}

== The smallest singular value ==
The smallest singular value of a matrix {{tmath|A}} is {{tmath|\sigma_\mathrm{n}(A)}}. For a non-singular matrix {{tmath|A}}, it has the following properties:

* <math>\left\| A^{-1} \right\|_2 = \sigma_\mathrm{n}^{-1}(A)</math>.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Demmel |first=James W. |url=http://epubs.siam.org/doi/book/10.1137/1.9781611971446 |title=Applied Numerical Linear Algebra |date=January 1997 |publisher=Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics |isbn=978-0-89871-389-3 |language=en |doi=10.1137/1.9781611971446}}.</ref>{{Rp|location=Thm.3.3}}
* For all indices {{tmath|1 \! \leq i, j \leq \! n}}, {{tmath|~}} {{tmath|\left\vert A_{i,j}^{-1} \right\vert \leq \sigma_\mathrm{n}^{-1}(A)}}.<ref name=":0" />{{Rp|location=Thm.3.3}}

Intuitively, if {{tmath|\sigma_\mathrm{n}(A)}} is small, then the rows of {{tmath|A}} are "almost" linearly dependent. If it is {{tmath|\sigma_\mathrm{n}(A) {{=}} 0}}, then the rows of {{tmath|A}} are linearly dependent and {{tmath|A}} is not invertible.

== Inequalities about singular values ==
See also:<ref>[[Roger Horn|R. A. Horn]] and [[Charles Royal Johnson|C. R. Johnson]]. Topics in Matrix Analysis. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, 1991. Chap. 3.</ref>

=== Singular values of sub-matrices ===
For {{tmath|A \in \C^{m \times n} }},
# Let <math>B</math> denote <math>A</math> with one of its rows ''or'' columns deleted. Then <math display="block">\sigma_{i+1}(A) \leq \sigma_i (B) \leq \sigma_i(A)</math>
# Let <math>B</math> denote <math>A</math> with two of its rows ''and'' columns deleted. Then <math display="block">\sigma_{i+2}(A) \leq \sigma_i (B) \leq \sigma_i(A)</math>
# Let <math>B</math> denote an <math>(m-k)\times(n-\ell)</math> submatrix of <math>A</math>. Then <math display="block">\sigma_{i+k+\ell}(A) \leq \sigma_i (B) \leq \sigma_i(A)</math>

=== Singular values of {{math|''A'' + ''B''}} ===
For {{tmath|A, B \in \C^{m \times n} }},
# <math display="block">\sum_{i=1}^k \sigma_i(A + B) \leq \sum_{i=1}^k \big( \sigma_i(A) + \sigma_i(B) \big), ~ \text{where} ~ k = \min \{m,n\}.</math>
# <math display="block">\sigma_{i+j-1}(A + B) \leq \sigma_i(A) + \sigma_j(B), \quad \forall \, i,j \in \N^*,\ i + j - 1 \leq \min \{m,n\}.</math>

=== Singular values of {{math|''AB''}} ===
For {{tmath|A, B \in \C^{n \times n} }},
# <math display="block">\begin{align}
  \prod_{i=n}^{i=n-k+1} \sigma_i(A) \sigma_i(B) &\leq \prod_{i=n}^{i=n-k+1} \sigma_i(AB). \\
                     \prod_{i=1}^k \sigma_i(AB) &\leq \prod_{i=1}^k \sigma_i(A) \sigma_i(B). \\
                    \sum_{i=1}^k \sigma_i^p(AB) &\leq \sum_{i=1}^k  \sigma_i^p(A) \sigma_i^p(B).
\end{align}</math>
# <math display="block">\sigma_n(A) \sigma_i(B) \leq \sigma_i (AB) \leq \sigma_1(A) \sigma_i(B), \quad \forall i = 1, 2, \ldots, n.</math>

For {{tmath|A, B \in \C^{m \times n} }},<ref>Eisenstat, S. C.; Ipsen, I. C. F. (1995). "Relative Perturbation Techniques for Singular Value Problems." SIAM Journal on Numerical Analysis. 32 (6): 1972–1988. doi:10.1137/0732088. p.1977</ref>
<math display="block">2 \sigma_i(A B^*) \leq \sigma_i \left( A^* A + B^* B \right), \quad \forall i = 1, 2, \ldots, n.</math>

=== Singular values and eigenvalues ===
For {{tmath|A \in \C^{n \times n} }},
# See:<ref>R. Bhatia. Matrix Analysis. Springer-Verlag, New York, 1997. Prop. III.5.1</ref>. <math display="block">\lambda_i \left( A + A^* \right) \leq 2 \sigma_i(A), \quad \forall i = 1, 2, \ldots, n.</math>
# Assume <math>\left| \lambda_1(A) \right| \geq \cdots \geq \left| \lambda_n(A) \right|</math>. Then for <math>k = 1, 2, \ldots, n</math>,
## [[Weyl's inequality#Weyl's inequality in matrix theory|Weyl's theorem]]: <math display="block">\prod_{i=1}^k \left| \lambda_i(A) \right| \leq \prod_{i=1}^k \sigma_i(A).</math>
## For <math>p>0</math>, <math display="block">\sum_{i=1}^k \left| \lambda_i^p(A) \right| \leq \sum_{i=1}^k \sigma_i^p(A).</math>

== History ==
This concept was introduced by [[Erhard Schmidt]] in 1907. Schmidt called singular values "eigenvalues" at that time. The name "singular value" was first quoted by Smithies in 1937. In 1957, Allahverdiev proved the following characterization of the {{tmath|n}}-th singular number:<ref>[[Israel Gohberg|I. C. Gohberg]] and [[Mark Krein|M. G. Krein]]. Introduction to the Theory of Linear Non-selfadjoint Operators. American Mathematical Society, Providence, R.I., 1969. Translated from the Russian by A. Feinstein. Translations of Mathematical Monographs, Vol. 18.</ref>
: <math>\sigma_n(T) = \inf \big\{ \, \|T-L\| : L \text{ is an operator of finite rank } < n \, \big\}.</math>

This formulation made it possible to extend the notion of singular values to operators in [[Banach space]]s.

Note that there is a more general concept of ''[[s-numbers]]'', which also includes Gelfand and Kolmogorov width.
